fields.name: GOST-yescrypt
fields.intro_template: yescrypt wrapped in Russia's national-standard Streebog HMAC. Same engine, different paperwork — the $gy$ prefix.

fields.prompt_template:
## GOST-yescrypt — a certified hash for a certified jurisdiction

The [yescrypt lesson](/algorithms/yescrypt/learn/the-default-nobody-noticed/) covered the hash that quietly became the Linux default: `$y$`, libxcrypt's memory-hard password hash. This lesson covers a variant of that same hash — one that exists for a reason that has nothing to do with cryptanalysis and everything to do with **law**.

### When "a good algorithm" isn't the whole requirement

Some jurisdictions don't just want a strong password hash — they want a **nationally certified** one. Russia is the clearest example: government systems, regulated industries, and increasingly general enterprise software are expected to use algorithms certified under the **GOST** standards (ГОСТ — *Gosudarstvennyi Standart*, "state standard"), the Russian Federation's national standards body's cryptographic suite. A perfectly good foreign-designed hash isn't an option on paper, however well it holds up in the literature.

### libxcrypt's answer: wrap, don't reinvent

Faced with that requirement, libxcrypt's maintainers didn't design a new memory-hard KDF from scratch for the Russian market. They took the yescrypt construction you already know — same `N`/`r` cost parameters, same ROMix-derived core — and wrapped its output with a GOST-certified hash function, **Streebog**. The result gets its own algorithm tag in the crypt string: `$gy$`, sitting right alongside `$y$` in libxcrypt's supported set.

```
$y$j9T$cloakcloakcloakcloakcloa$LKHGDskzibNHFZqsGMn5nyWnZe8ofXjcNOzlWJCtVN8
$gy$j9T$cloakcloakcloakcloakcloa$bx7Lod.gilIKA2u0XtVQER2Wh.A38WNp7.TeHPI6XU8
```

(The `$gy$` line is one character longer than the `$y$` line, purely because the tag itself is longer — everything after the second `$` lines up field-for-field.) Same password, same salt, same cost parameters — different prefix, different hash bytes. That pair is real output from `crypt(3)`; you'll spot exactly what changed in step 4.

### Where you'd actually meet this

`$gy$` shows up in **Russian government IT systems**, regulated Russian enterprise deployments, and distributions built for that market — most visibly **Astra Linux**, a Russian Linux distribution used across government and defense-adjacent institutions, which ships GOST-certified crypto as a first-class requirement rather than an afterthought. If you're not operating in that regulatory environment, you'll likely never type `$gy$` — but it's a good case study in a pattern that shows up anywhere compliance meets cryptography: how do you satisfy a certification requirement without throwing away a well-analyzed design?
fields.help_template: **In plain English:** GOST-yescrypt (`$gy$`) is libxcrypt's yescrypt hash with a Russian national-standard hash function, Streebog, wrapped around its output — built for jurisdictions (chiefly Russia) that require GOST-certified cryptography by law. Same cost parameters and salt handling as plain yescrypt; different certification story. You'll meet it on Russian government systems and distros like Astra Linux, rarely anywhere else.

fields.prompt_template:
### Streebog — Russia's SHA-2 analog

**GOST R 34.11-2012**, nicknamed **Streebog** after Stribog, a Slavic deity associated with the winds, is Russia's national-standard cryptographic hash function. It was adopted in 2012 and became mandatory in Russian systems from 2013 onward, replacing the older GOST R 34.11-94 hash. Functionally, it plays the same role in Russia's GOST suite that SHA-2 plays in NIST's: the default "just hash this" primitive that everything else — HMAC constructions, signature schemes, key derivation — gets built on top of.

### Shape of the construction

| Property | Streebog |
|---|---|
| Digest sizes | **256-bit** and **512-bit** variants |
| Overall shape | Merkle–Damgård-like: message processed in blocks, chained through a compression function |
| Compression function | Built around an **LPS** round — **L**inear transformation, **P**ermutation, **S**ubstitution — repeated across 12 rounds per block, wrapped in a Miyaguchi–Preneel-style feedback |
| Block size | 512 bits |

The LPS round is the distinctive piece: each round applies an S-box substitution (byte-wise, non-linear), a permutation (shuffling byte positions), and a linear transformation (an MDS-like matrix multiply over GF(2)) — a structure with a similar flavor to AES's SubBytes/ShiftRows/MixColumns, repurposed as a hash compression step rather than a block cipher round.

### How much scrutiny has it had?

Streebog has been picked apart in the **international** cryptographic literature since shortly after standardization — academic papers have examined it for rebound attacks, collision search shortcuts on reduced-round variants, and structural weaknesses. None of that work has produced a **practical break** of the full, standard-round hash. That's a genuinely reassuring track record — but it's worth being precise about what it does and doesn't mean: Streebog is a *nationally* standardized hash that has been *internationally* analyzed, which is a different claim from being an internationally *adopted* standard the way SHA-256 is. Outside contexts where GOST compliance is required, you won't find Streebog as anyone's default choice.

### The part that matters for this lesson

GOST-yescrypt doesn't ask Streebog to be a *password* hash on its own. Streebog isn't the thing standing between an attacker and a cracked credential — the expensive work is all upstream in yescrypt, and Streebog's job (as the next step details) is to feed into an HMAC construction wrapped around that already-expensive computation. For that job, Streebog just needs to be a solid, collision-resistant general-purpose hash — which the record above supports. The actual password-cracking resistance in GOST-yescrypt still comes entirely from **yescrypt's memory-hardness**, exactly as it does in plain `$y$`. Streebog changes the paperwork, not the security model.
fields.help_template: **In plain English:** Streebog (GOST R 34.11-2012) is Russia's national-standard hash function — 256/512-bit digests, a Merkle–Damgård-like design built around a 12-round LPS (linear/permutation/substitution) compression step. It's been studied internationally with no practical break found, though it's a nationally-mandated standard rather than a globally adopted one like SHA-256. In GOST-yescrypt it's only asked to be a solid HMAC hash — the actual cracking resistance still comes from yescrypt's memory-hardness.

fields.prompt_template:
### The construction: wrap, don't reinvent

Here's the whole idea as a flow:

```
password ──▶ yescrypt(N, r, salt) ──▶ HMAC-Streebog-256 ──▶ $gy$ hash
```

Read left to right:

1. **`yescrypt(N, r, salt)`** — run the exact same memory-hard construction from the [yescrypt lesson](/algorithms/yescrypt/learn/the-default-nobody-noticed/), with the same cost parameters `N` (blocks) and `r` (block-size multiplier) and the same salt. This step is untouched — all the ROMix fill-then-wander work, all the memory-hardness, is identical to plain `$y$`.
2. **`HMAC-Streebog-256`** — take yescrypt's output and run it through an HMAC construction that uses Streebog-256 as its inner hash function, instead of the SHA-2/SHA-3 family you'd see in a typical HMAC. This is a comparatively cheap, fast step — it's not where the cost lives.
3. **`$gy$` hash** — the HMAC output becomes the hash bytes stored after the `$gy$` tag.

### What passes through unchanged

Look back at the pair from step 1:

```
$y$j9T$cloakcloakcloakcloakcloa$LKHGDskzibNHFZqsGMn5nyWnZe8ofXjcNOzlWJCtVN8
$gy$j9T$cloakcloakcloakcloakcloa$bx7Lod.gilIKA2u0XtVQER2Wh.A38WNp7.TeHPI6XU8
```

The cost-parameter tag (`j9T`) and the salt (`cloakcloakcloakcloakcloa`) are byte-for-byte identical between the two lines. That's the construction working as designed: salt and cost parameters pass straight through to yescrypt exactly as before, completely unaffected by the Streebog wrapping. Only the algorithm tag and the final hash bytes differ — because the hash bytes are no longer yescrypt's raw output, they're that output re-processed through HMAC-Streebog-256.

### Why wrapping beats reinventing

yescrypt has roughly **ten years** of public analysis behind it: a Password Hashing Competition finalist, deployed as a Linux distro default since 2021, picked apart by the same community that stress-tests every major password hash. Designing a brand-new GOST-certified memory-hard KDF from scratch would throw all of that away and start the clock over — new construction, new unknowns, years before anyone could trust it the way they trust yescrypt today.

Wrapping is the cheaper, safer move: keep the well-analyzed memory-hard core completely intact, and bolt the certified primitive on as a **post-processing step** that satisfies the compliance requirement without touching the part of the design that actually does the security work.

### The general lesson

This pattern isn't specific to Russia or to Streebog. It's the standard playbook whenever a regulator mandates a specific approved primitive: **don't rebuild the whole system around the mandated piece — find the smallest wrapper that satisfies the requirement while leaving your battle-tested core alone.** The same move shows up wherever FIPS-approved algorithms get bolted onto existing designs, or wherever a national standard has to coexist with an internationally vetted one.
fields.help_template: **In plain English:** GOST-yescrypt runs the password through ordinary yescrypt first — same cost parameters, same salt, same memory-hard work — then pipes that output through HMAC-Streebog-256 to produce the final hash bytes. Salt and cost parameters pass through unchanged; only the prefix and hash bytes differ from plain `$y$`. Wrapping a certified primitive around a well-analyzed core is cheaper and safer than reinventing the whole KDF to satisfy a compliance requirement.

fields.prompt_template:
### Spot the difference

Here's a real `$y$`/`$gy$` pair, generated from the **same password** and the **same salt**:

```
$y$j9T$cloakcloakcloakcloakcloa$LKHGDskzibNHFZqsGMn5nyWnZe8ofXjcNOzlWJCtVN8
$gy$j9T$cloakcloakcloakcloakcloa$bx7Lod.gilIKA2u0XtVQER2Wh.A38WNp7.TeHPI6XU8
```

Same password. Same salt. Same cost parameters. One line runs through plain yescrypt; the other runs the same yescrypt output through HMAC-Streebog-256 before it gets encoded, as you saw in the previous step.

**Which field actually changed between the two lines?** Pick one: the salt, the cost parameters, or the prefix + hash bytes. Look carefully at the two strings above before you choose — the answer is visible in the text, not something you need to compute.
fields.help_template: **In plain English:** Compare the two hash strings character by character. The salt field (`cloakcloakcloakcloakcloa`) and the parameter tag (`j9T`) are identical in both — the construction from the previous step passes those through to yescrypt unchanged. What differs is the algorithm tag (`$y$` vs `$gy$`) and everything after the last `$` — the hash bytes themselves, because the `$gy$` line ran yescrypt's output through an extra HMAC-Streebog-256 step before encoding it.

fields.prompt_template:
### When to actually reach for `$gy$`

The honest scoping, no hedging:

| Situation | Pick |
|---|---|
| A regulator or law mandates GOST-certified cryptography for your system | **`$gy$`** — it's the certified answer, and it costs you nothing in memory-hardness versus plain yescrypt. |
| Everyone else | **Plain `$y$` yescrypt, or Argon2id** |

That's the whole decision tree. If you're not operating under a GOST compliance requirement, `$gy$` gives you **no security advantage** over plain yescrypt — the cracking resistance comes from the identical memory-hard yescrypt core either way, and Streebog is along for the compliance ride, not doing extra security work. What `$gy$` *does* cost you, outside a GOST context, is ecosystem size: fewer tutorials, fewer libraries with first-class support, fewer engineers who've seen it before, and a smaller pool of independent cryptanalysis specifically targeting the wrapped construction (as opposed to yescrypt and Streebog individually, which are each reasonably well studied on their own).

### Portability isn't guaranteed

`$gy$` support isn't guaranteed just because you're running libxcrypt. Whether `crypt(3)` on a given system can produce or verify `$gy$` hashes depends on the `--enable-hashes` build-time flag libxcrypt was compiled with — specifically, whether the GOST hashes were included in that build's enabled set. **Fedora and RHEL enable it by default**, and it's not an exotic add-on either way — libxcrypt vendors its own Streebog implementation, so distributions that enable it aren't pulling in an extra external dependency to do so. It's simply a build-time choice some distributions make and others don't.

The practical consequence: if you're deploying `$gy$` hashes, verify the *target* system's libxcrypt was built with GOST support before you rely on it — don't assume it travels with "any Linux box running libxcrypt" the way `$y$` effectively does.
fields.help_template: **In plain English:** Use `$gy$` if a regulator requires GOST-certified crypto — that's genuinely the only reason to reach for it. Otherwise plain yescrypt or Argon2id is the better choice: same security either way, but a bigger ecosystem and no compliance overhead. And `$gy$` isn't universally available — it depends on whether the target system's libxcrypt was built with GOST support (Fedora/RHEL: yes by default; not every distro).

fields.prompt_template:
## Done!

You've walked GOST-yescrypt end to end — why a nationally-certified hash exists at all, what Streebog actually is, how it wraps around yescrypt without touching the memory-hard core, spotting exactly what changes between `$y$` and `$gy$`, and when `$gy$` is (and isn't) the right call.

### Recap

| Step | Key idea |
|---|---|
| 1 (intro) | Some jurisdictions (Russia: GOST) legally require certified crypto. libxcrypt's answer: wrap yescrypt instead of reinventing it. Tag `$gy$`. |
| 2 (Streebog) | GOST R 34.11-2012, Russia's SHA-2 analog — 256/512-bit, Merkle–Damgård-like with a 12-round LPS compression step. Internationally analyzed, no practical breaks, but a national rather than globally-adopted standard. |
| 3 (the wrapper) | `password → yescrypt(N, r, salt) → HMAC-Streebog-256 → $gy$ hash`. Salt and cost parameters pass through unchanged. Wrapping preserves yescrypt's decade of analysis instead of discarding it. |
| 4 (spot the difference) | Same salt, same params, both lines — only the prefix and hash bytes differ. |
| 5 (when to use) | GOST mandate → `$gy$`. Otherwise plain yescrypt or Argon2id — no security upside, smaller ecosystem, and support isn't universal (Fedora/RHEL: yes; not every distro). |

### The codegen

Click **Show full script** below. It's the same dependency-free Python pattern from the yescrypt lesson — `ctypes` calling your system's real `crypt(3)` — but requesting a `$gy$` hash instead of `$y$`. It'll only produce a genuine GOST hash if your system's libxcrypt was built with GOST support; otherwise `crypt()` returns `None`. libxcrypt fails closed on an unsupported prefix — it never silently falls back to a weaker algorithm — which is exactly the behavior you want from a compliance-driven hash: a broken `$gy$` request should be loud, not quietly downgraded.

### In the real world

- **Check support the way the script does, not by reading docs.** The `crypt(5)` man page documents the `$gy$` method, but it's a static reference — it lists the method whether or not *your* build actually supports it, so it can't tell you what your system will do. The check that actually works is the one the codegen above performs: attempt a `crypt()` call with a `$gy$` setting string and see whether you get a hash back or `None`.
- **Fedora and RHEL enable GOST support at build time.** If you're targeting those distributions (or Astra Linux, which is built around GOST compliance from the ground up), `$gy$` is available out of the box. Elsewhere, check first.
- **Don't reach for `$gy$` unless compliance requires it.** Plain yescrypt (`$y$`) or Argon2id remain the better default anywhere GOST certification isn't a legal or contractual requirement.
fields.help_template: **In plain English:** GOST-yescrypt = plain yescrypt's memory-hard core, unchanged, with its output re-hashed through HMAC-Streebog-256 to satisfy Russia's GOST certification requirement. Salt and cost parameters pass straight through; only the prefix and final hash bytes change. Use it only when GOST compliance is mandated — verify support on your target system with a real `crypt()` call using a `$gy$` setting (not the `crypt(5)` man page, which lists the method regardless of build flags); support depends on `--enable-hashes` at build time (Fedora/RHEL: on by default).
